newsitem.title: USA: Miami grand jury indicts three in arms smuggle plot.
newsitem.headline: Miami grand jury indicts three in arms smuggle plot.

text.p: A U.S. grand jury in Miami has indicted two Lithuanians and a Cypriot on charges of plotting to smuggle surface-to-air missiles and other military weapons into the United States, federal prosecutors said on Thursday.
The grand jury returned a three-count indictment against Alexander Darichev, Aleksandr Pogrebezskij and Angelo Zeini.

The indictments charged that they negotiated to sell the weapons to U.S. undercover agents posing as Russian and Ukrainian nationals working for Colombian drug lords, the Miami U.S. Attorney's Office said in a statement.
When the U.S. Customs Service announced the arrest of Darichev and Pogrebezskij on June 30, it said the men also had asked the undercover agents if they were interested in tactical nuclear weapons.

The indictment alleged that Pogrebezskij, 28, and Darichev, 36, schemed to import weapons of mass destruction through front companies including Phoenix Arms International and Zodiac, Inc., the statement said.
Both men were accused of offering to bribe foreign officials to make it appear that the missile systems were being bought by the Lithuanian Ministry of Defence, it said.

Zeini, a Cypriot, was charged with creating false paperwork to indicate that a shipment was machinery and general cargo destined for Puerto Rico rather than missile systems enroute to Lithuania, it said.
The suspects said the weapons would be supplied by Armimex, a Bulgarian government munitions supplier that had been licensed by the former Soviet Union to produce weapons during the Cold War.

Bulgaria's trade ministry denied wrongdoing in the case. It said a legal license was issued in December 1996 for Armimex to export weapons to the United States firm Phoenix Arms International for delivery to the Lithuanian defence ministry, but the deal was not completed because the buyer was unable to pay.
Darichev and Pogrebezskij also allegedly laundered $50,000 from bank accounts in Palm Beach, Florida, and New York through Lithuania.
On July 2, a top Lithuanian police official dismissed the suspects as "swindlers," saying they could not have had access to nuclear weapons.
If convicted they could face 35 years in prison and fines up to $1 million.
